boundary_rationale: A disjunctive nominal opening ('Now the sons of Eli were wicked men,' 2:12) pivots the topic away from the resumptive ministering-refrain verse and introduces one continuous iterative description of the priests' fork-custom (2:13-14) escalating into the servant's coercive demand and threat of forced seizure (2:15-16, gam beterem continuing the same iterative mode rather than opening a new register), closing on the narrator's own verdict, 'The sin of the young men was very great before Yahweh' (2:17). This merges the formerly separate M8-1Sam-008 (2:12-2:14) and M8-1Sam-009 (2:15-2:17): the seam previously drawn at 2:14|2:15 rested only on a WEB paragraph marker at 2:16 (one verse later than the drafted cut) and on misattributing 2:16's seizure threat to 2:15, neither of which supports a division at 2:14|2:15. The unit's own edges are independently marked: a disjunctive nominal clause opens it at 2:12, and 2:18's adversative uShemuel mesharet ('But Samuel ministered') closes it with a clean contrastive pivot.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the fork-custom description (2:12-14) from the coercion-and-verdict material (2:15-17) was considered, since a register shift from description to direct speech does occur inside the unit, but 2:15 opens with the additive gam continuing the same iterative verb pattern as 2:13-14 with no WEB paragraph break before it, so the shift is internal color rather than a seam; the real coercion language ('I will take it by force') is delayed to 2:16, one verse past the strongest candidate internal cut, further undermining any split at 2:14/2:15.

boundary_rationale: This verse is a refrain-and-variation on the growth notice of v.21b, not a near-verbatim restatement: 2:21b is a single wayyiqtol (vayigdal hanaar Shemuel im YHWH), while 2:26 is a disjunctive waw-plus-subject-plus-participial-chain (vehanaar Shemuel holech vegadel vatov gam im YHWH vegam im anashim) that adds vatov and an entire second gam-clause extending favor to human beings; the two share only the na'ar-Shemuel subject, the g-d-l root, and im YHWH. strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating it as the opening verse of the oracle unit was considered since it precedes v.27 directly, but its content and vocabulary belong entirely to the preceding growth-notice pattern, not to the messenger-formula speech that follows.

boundary_rationale: This is a bounded type-scene built on threefold repetition -- Yahweh calls, Samuel runs to Eli, Eli sends him back -- climaxing in Eli's coaching (3:9) and the fourth call (3:10), closed by Samuel's changed response 'Speak; for your servant hears.' The scene now opens on its own vayehi bayom hahu temporal onset (3:2), keeping the protasis (the circumstantial chain of 3:2-3: Eli's failing eyes, the unextinguished lamp, Samuel lying in the temple) together with its apodosis (the first call at 3:4) rather than splitting them at 3:3|3:4, which fell mid-construction. The rear edge is unchanged and strong: 3:10 completes the fourfold pattern and 3:11 shifts into sustained oracular speech.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Cutting the pattern into three separate call-and-response units was considered but rejected, since the campaign's binding rules treat a repeated type-scene as one bounded unit rather than atomizing each iteration. Retaining the seam at 3:3|3:4 (the original draft) was also considered but rejected because it divides a single suspended construction (vayehi bayom hahu ... circumstantial clauses ... vayiqra) at a point internal to it, evidenced by WEB's own trailing commas at 3:2 and 3:3.

boundary_rationale: The chapter closes with a generalizing summary formula ('Samuel grew... let none of his words fall to the ground... All Israel... knew that Samuel was established to be a prophet') that steps outside scene-time entirely. This is a durative, office-establishment notice, not a regnal accession formula (no age, reign-length, or death formula is present, unlike the true accession notice at 13:1), so the tag is corrected to narrative_prose. The front edge against Samuel's dialogue is unmistakable. The rear edge is genuinely contested rather than settled: 4:1a (vayehi devar Shemuel lechol Yisrael) shares the devar catchword and durative, all-Israel register with 3:19/3:21, and WEB's own paragraph break falls mid-verse inside 4:1, after the devar-clause and before the battle report - grouping 4:1a with this unit rather than with what follows. But 4:1a is also bound forward to 4:1b by a wayyiqtol chain (vayehi...vayetze Yisra'el) with no disjunctive marker, which pulls toward the battle narrative - though the chain's second verb re-expresses its subject (vayetze Yisra'el names Israel explicitly, rather than continuing on an implicit subject), a construction this campaign elsewhere treats as its own boundary-relevant signal (045's 9:5 hemmah ba'u, 057's vehinneh Sha'ul ba), which weakens, without eliminating, this forward pull as a counterweight to the devar-catchword reading. Since the grammar genuinely supports both readings, this decision discloses the devar-chain reading as a live, unresolved alternative rather than silently asserting the drafted cut, and downgrades confidence accordingly.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the span to 1Sam.3.19-1Sam.4.1 to keep the devar-catchword material together, on the strength of the shared vocabulary with 3:19/3:21 and WEB's mid-verse paragraph break after 4:1a, is a live and undecided alternative rather than a rejected one: 4:1a is genuinely Janus-faced, bound backward by register and catchword and forward by a wayyiqtol chain with no disjunctive marker, though that forward pull is weakened (not eliminated) by the chain's second verb re-expressing its subject (vayetze Yisra'el) rather than continuing null-subject. Folding this into the preceding dialogue (i.e. not isolating the summary at all) remains rejected, since the shift from scene-bound speech to durative, all-Israel-scope narration is a real register-driven signal.

boundary_rationale: The elders' rhetorical question and resulting decision to fetch the ark from Shiloh (4:3) forms a short deliberation scene that closes with the ark's dispatch and removal from Shiloh, and the notice that Eli's two sons were there with it (4:4: vayishlach ha'am Shiloh vayis'u misham et aron...vesham shenei venei Eli). The unit closes on this removal-from-Shiloh notice, not on an arrival at the camp -- the ark's arrival at the camp is narrated only in the next verse (4:5, vayehi kevo aron...el hammachaneh), which belongs to a separate unit. The real closing signal is the shift in narrative vantage from the dispatching party (Shiloh) to the camp about to receive the ark. WEB opens a paragraph at 4:4, grouping 4:3 with the preceding battle report rather than with this unit -- an untested alternative front edge worth noting even though the elders' single deliberation (question-and-decision) still reads most naturally as one unit with its own dispatch.

Splitting at 4:3|4:4 to follow WEB's paragraph start at 4:4 is a live untested alternative, but the elders' single continuous deliberation (question in 4:3, decision-and-dispatch in 4:4) argues against fragmenting it.

boundary_rationale: The Philistines summon their priests and diviners and ask what to do with Yahweh's ark (6:2); the priests answer without any intervening pause (6:3, im meshallechim), opening one continuous consultation exchange with internal turn-taking that runs through the trespass-offering instruction, the Egypt/Pharaoh warning, and the diagnostic experimental design (new cart, unyoked cows, calves shut away), closing on 'it was a chance that happened to us' (6:9). This merges the formerly separate M8-1Sam-029 (6:3-6:6) and M8-1Sam-030 (6:7-6:9), and additionally draws 6:2 in from the old M8-1Sam-028: 6:2's question and 6:3's answer are one dialogue turn under the turn-marker principle and cannot be split. A second such turn occurs at 6:4, which itself contains two vayyomru frames - the Philistines' own question, mah ha'asham asher nashiv lo ('What should the trespass offering be which we shall return to him?'), answered by the priests' reply, mispar sarnei Pelishtim ('Five golden tumors and five golden mice, for the number of the lords of the Philistines...') - a genuine speaker exchange, but under the same turn-marker principle it is an internal Q&A turn inside one uninterrupted consultation scene, not a unit boundary: the same two parties remain in view, no relocation occurs, and the priests' answer at 6:4 continues directly into the same instruction that runs through 6:9. Likewise 6:7's ve'attah ('and now') is a discourse-internal pivot inside the still-running speech begun at 6:4b, not a new utterance - WEB's re-opened quotation mark at 6:7 is a typographic convention for continued direct speech, not evidence of a fresh speech act. The unit's front edge is the durative-to-action shift from the preceding 6:1 notice; its rear edge is genuinely strong - 6:10 turns to vaya'asu ha'anashim ken, a wayyiqtol with an explicit subject supplying both a compliance formula and a participant refocus.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the trespass-offering instruction from the Egypt warning, or the theological warning from the concrete cart-and-cows procedure, was considered, but all of it is one uninterrupted consultation by the same speakers answering the same question. Internal turn-taking occurs at 6:4, where the Philistines' question and the priests' answer form a genuine Q&A exchange, but this turn does not reset the scene or relocate either party, and is not itself promoted to a unit boundary under the turn-marker principle; the only genuine reset in the neighborhood is 6:10's compliance formula. boundary_rationale: This span deliberately crosses the chapter line. The front edge is marked by the shift from the narrator's own to-this-day deictic close (6:18) to the resuming wayyiqtol vayach at 6:19 ('Yahweh struck the men of Beth Shemesh'), opening a new and darker beat. The rear edge is not, as previously claimed, an absence of any intervening scene break between the Kiriath Jearim invitation (6:21) and its fulfillment (7:1) -- WEB in fact opens paragraphs at both 6:21 and 7:1, and 7:1 introduces new participants (anshei Qiryat Ye'arim) at a new location (beit Avinadav bagiv'ah). The genuine rear-edge signal is instead the twenty-year jump at 7:2 (vayirbu hayamim vayihyu esrim shanah), corroborated by the pe sited after 7:1; the request-and-fulfillment continuity between 6:21 and 7:1 (the messengers' invitation answered directly by the men of Kiriath Jearim's action, with no renewed deliberation) is a real but secondary consideration for keeping the chapter-crossing span whole, not the absence of any marked break.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Bracketing 1Sam.6.21-1Sam.7.1 as its own unit (corroborated by the samekh sited after 6:20 and the pe sited after 7:1) was not previously tested and is recorded here as the live rejected alternative: it is textually available, since both verses carry participant/location signals of their own, but the request-and-fulfillment link between the messengers' invitation and its narrated completion, plus the shared 7:2 rear boundary, favor keeping 6:19-7:1 as one span over fragmenting the ark's-return material further.

boundary_rationale: A durative time-marker ('the time was long -- for it was twenty years') opens a new phase of national mourning, Samuel's reform call to abandon foreign gods, and the Mizpah water-pouring repentance ritual, closing with the summary note that Samuel judged Israel there. 7:2's opening clause is itself backward-referencing (vayehi miyom shevet ha'aron beQiryat Ye'arim, tying it to the ark's resting place just narrated at 7:1) before pivoting to the durative, all-Israel-scope 'twenty years... lamented' language that actually opens the reform movement -- this Janus-faced quality is disclosed here as a live alternative affiliation (7:2 could in principle close the preceding ark unit) rather than treated as settled. The span is nonetheless kept whole because 7:5 (Samuel's 'gather all Israel to Mizpah') is the same speech-act that convenes the assembly narrated at 7:6, binding the duration notice to the repentance ritual it introduces. A samekh sited after 7:2 gives weak corroboration and does not by itself decide the question.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Separating Samuel's reform speech (vv.3-4) from the Mizpah assembly (vv.5-6) was considered, but the speech directly sets up the assembly it calls for, and both belong to a single continuous movement toward national repentance. Also disclosed as live rather than settled: reading 7:2 as the closing verse of the preceding ark-at-Kiriath-Jearim unit (M8-1Sam-035) rather than as this unit's own opening, on the strength of its backward-referencing clause -- not adopted, since the assembly-convening link from 7:5 to 7:6 argues for keeping 7:2 with the reform movement it introduces.

boundary_rationale: Samuel's stone-setting and its Ebenezer etiology open a summarizing coda to the battle, broadening out to a generalized report of Philistine subjugation and restored borders that closes the war narrative before the office-summary notice begins. boundary_rationale: The elders convene and voice the kingship demand, Samuel's displeasure leads to prayer, and Yahweh's response reframes the demand as a rejection of divine kingship while instructing Samuel to warn the people (8:9, vehiggadta lahem mishpat hammelekh) - a complete request-and-divine-response cycle. The seam falls at 8:10|8:11: v.11 opens the warning's actual content with its own fronted demonstrative declaration, vayomer zeh yihyeh mishpat hammelekh ('This will be the way of the king who shall reign over you'), a fronted-predicate construction distinct from v.10's report-frame vayomer and paralleling the fronted-object-plus-yiqqach morphology M8-1Sam-042 uses to argue its own opening at this same edge. The unit accordingly runs 8:4-8:10, closing on the discharge of Yahweh's instruction rather than on the instruction itself, before the catalogue of the king's practices begins at 8:11.

boundary_rationale: Samuel's 'manner of the king' speech opens on its own introductory formula, zeh yihyeh mishpat hammelech ('This will be the way of the king,' 8:11) -- not 8:10, which is narratorial attribution ('Samuel told all Yahweh's words to the people') containing no enumeration. The catalog is a two-verb alternation, not uniform anaphora as previously claimed: a fronted-object-plus-yiqqach pattern at 8:11, 8:13, 8:14, and 8:16 (military conscription, land seizure, produce), alternating with the distinct verb ya'sor ('he will tithe') at 8:15 and 8:17; 8:12 has no finite taking verb at all (velasum lo sarei alafim); and 8:18 breaks the pattern completely with a second-person consequence clause (uze'aqtem bayom hahu, 'you will cry out in that day'). WEB's rendering of ya'sor as 'he will take one tenth of' had manufactured a false uniformity. The catalog closes at 8:18 and 8:19 resumes narrative (vayemaanu ha'am, 'the people refused'). A samekh sited after both 8:9 and 8:10 weakly corroborates 8:10 standing apart from the catalog it precedes; 8:10 itself needs separate attachment (to the preceding deliberation-cycle unit or as a standalone hinge), which lies outside this half's assigned decisions.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Breaking the catalog into thematic sub-lists (military conscription, land, tithes) was considered, but the two-verb alternation (yiqqach/ya'sor) runs across all the thematic groupings without any accompanying formula reset, so splitting by theme would manufacture seams the text does not itself mark. Including 8:10 in the span was also considered and rejected, since 8:10 is narratorial report with no enumeration, one verse before the catalog's own introductory formula.

boundary_rationale: The donkeys go missing and Kish sends Saul out; the search widens through several districts (9:3-9:4) into the land of Zuph (9:5, hemmah bau be'eretz Tsuf), where Saul proposes turning back - and the servant's counter-proposal to consult the man of God (9:6), Saul's objection about the missing gift (9:7), and the servant's silver offer (9:8) are three turns of one continuous negotiation between the same two participants, with no relocation and no participant change anywhere in the stretch. This merges the formerly separate M8-1Sam-045 (9:3-9:5) and M8-1Sam-046 (9:6-9:8): the 9:5|9:6 seam previously drawn between them was a bare speaker-change turn, justified only by the servant's idea 'redirecting the plot' - a content judgment, not a text signal, and inconsistent with how this same unit correctly declines to split its own three internal turns: 9:6 and 9:7 open on a bare vayomer, while 9:8 opens instead on a yasaph-plus-infinitive continuation frame, vayyosef hanna'ar la'anot et Sha'ul vayomer ('the young man continued answering Saul, and said'), a stronger, different formula that intensifies rather than merely repeats the pattern - all three nonetheless carry WEB paragraph starts. The unit closes cleanly at 9:9, a register break of the first order (the narrator's aside on the seer/prophet terminology, set off by parentheses in translation).
strongest_rejected_alternative: 9:4|9:5 was tested as an internal candidate seam: 9:5's fronted-pronoun-plus-qatal circumstantial construction (hemmah bau) paired with relocation into Zuph and a shift into direct speech is a stronger formal signal than the 9:5|9:6 speaker-change turn this unit used to be cut at, but it falls within one continuous search-and-negotiation movement (the donkeys are still the subject at hand through 9:5's own proposal to turn back) and is not promoted to a boundary.

Verse 17 is therefore better described as the flashback's resumption into present narrated time (Samuel actually seeing Saul, Yahweh's confirming word) than as still part of the flashback itself - consistent with the observation that v.17 completes the clause v.14 left hanging and hands the narrative forward into the encounter that follows, rather than closing a retrospective panel.

boundary_rationale: A new location and threat opens the chapter -- Nahash's siege of Jabesh Gilead and his demand of mutilation -- and the elders negotiate a seven-day reprieve and propose dispatching messengers 'in all the borders of Israel' (11:3). This unit now extends through the messengers' dispatch itself: 11:4 (vayavou hamalachim Giv'at Shaul) discharges the elders' proposal with a bare wayyiqtol whose subject (hamalachim) is anaphoric to the 'messengers' just named, not an independent scene-opener. The genuine off-chain construction that re-introduces an absent participant -- vehinneh Shaul ba, waw-presentative plus named subject plus participle, the only such construction in the chapter -- falls one verse later, at 11:5, walking Saul back onto the page after his absence since chapter 10 closed. The boundary is therefore moved to 11:4|11:5, keeping the elders' decision to dispatch messengers together with its immediate discharge.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Ending this unit at 11:3, with 'the messengers came' (11:4) opening the next scene, was the drafted position and is now rejected: 11:4's wayyiqtol has no independent subject of its own and simply completes the plan proposed one clause earlier, so cutting there splits a plan from its discharge at the weakest marker available, while the chapter's only waw-presentative construction sits untested one verse further on. boundary_rationale: Samuel opens a formal farewell address with a self-presentation and an offer to be cross-examined for wrongdoing ('Here I am. Witness against me before Yahweh,' 12:1-3), and the people's exoneration (12:4), Samuel's witness-formula invoking Yahweh and the king (12:5a), and the closing exchange (12:5b) are the solicited response that same challenge explicitly calls for, not an independently initiated speech-act. This merges the formerly separate M8-1Sam-061 (12:1-12:3) and M8-1Sam-062 (12:4-12:5): the 12:3|12:4 seam previously drawn between them was a bare vayomeru turn marker, morphologically identical to the vayomer/vayomeru turns at 12:5 (twice) and 12:6, two of which the draft itself correctly treats as internal to a unit - an inconsistent application of the turn-marker principle. Chapter 12 as a whole is further textured by a near-verbatim inclusio bracketing the larger address: 12:2's ve'attah hinneh hammelekh mithhallekh lifneikhem is answered almost word for word at 12:13's ve'attah hinneh hammelekh asher becharttem. This inclusio is context for the chapter's overall rhetorical shape, not a boundary warrant for this unit's own span, since taken as a bracket it would run past this decision's own rear edge at 12:5; the case for closing here rests instead on the pe (two-witness) sited after 12:5 and the oath-of-clearance's own formal closure, with 12:6 opening a fresh topic marker (the historical recital) that begins the next unit. Note on 12:5's own closing clause: MT prints vayomer ed, third-masculine-singular with no expressed plural subject - 'he said, Witness' - while WEB renders the clause with a plural subject, 'They said, He is witness,' not present in MT; the seal is Samuel's own single-voice formula, not a chorused assembly response.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating 12:1-3 (the challenge) and 12:4-5 (the exoneration) as two independently-bounded speech-acts, on the grounds that they are spoken by different parties, was the drafted position and is now rejected: this is exactly the situation the turn-marker principle (illustrated at 1:9-18) says should be resisted absent an independent scene or topic change, and the campaign's own recalibration already declined an identical rhetorical-function-only warrant. boundary_rationale: Samuel's address opens on a nominal predication about Yahweh (12:6, 'It is Yahweh who appointed Moses and Aaron') that introduces, but is not itself, the historical recital: the recital's own content begins only at 12:8 (ka'asher ba Ya'akov Mitzrayim), with 12:7 functioning as a distinct lawsuit-form element, the summons (ve'attah hityatzevu ve'ishaftah, reflexive imperative plus cohortative of judgment) - confirmed as a separable element by its own partial verbal echo at 12:16 (gam attah hityatzevu ur'u): only 'attah hityatzevu' recurs from 12:7's ve'attah hityatzevu, with a different opening particle (gam vs. ve-) and a different second verb (ur'u vs. ve'ishaftah). The unit's far edge is weaker than previously rated: 12:12 opens with vatiru, a second-plural wayyiqtol continuing the same address to the same audience; the pivot from the era of the judges to the recent Ammonite crisis is a topic change inside one continuous speech, not an independently text-evidenced seam.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the recital through the present-day indictment (vv.12-15) was considered and remains rejected, since v.12 pivots from past history to the present crisis, a recognizable topic shift even though it carries no independent text signal of its own. Separating the summons (12:6-7) from the recital proper (12:8-11) into two decisions was also considered; it is not adopted, since both remain part of one continuous covenant-lawsuit address bounded by the same speaker and audience, but the summons is noted as its own form-element within the span rather than folded silently into 'the recital's own introduction.'

boundary_rationale: This verse is the book's own accession formula, closed in form (subject plus accession-infinitive clause, ben shanah Shaul bemalcho, followed by a reign-length clause, ushtei shanim malach al Yisrael), sharing nothing with Samuel's peroration that ends chapter 12 or with the wayyiqtol muster that begins at 13:2. As printed, MT is not blank or damaged at the accession-age slot -- it reads ben shanah ('a son of one year'), an anomalous but present value. WEB's own footnote discloses that the traditional Hebrew text omits both 'thirty' (the tens digit of Saul's age) and 'forty-' (the tens digit of the forty-two-year reign length), with both numerals supplied from a few Septuagint manuscripts; this is a doubly reconstructed verse, not a single damaged figure. Both edges are form-marked, and a pe after 12:25 corroborates the near one.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this into the muster account (vv.2-7) as its introductory date-notice was considered, but the formula's closed regnal shape ('became king... reigned... years') matches the accession-notice pattern used elsewhere in the history and is anomalous (not merely a narrative lead-in) in a way that marks it as its own unit.

boundary_rationale: Saul's seven-day wait, his unauthorized offering just as Samuel arrives, and Samuel's confrontation form the first rejection oracle of the book, closing on the announcement that Yahweh has sought 'a man after his own heart.' The rear edge is genuinely strong: a completed verdict at 13:14, answered at 13:15 by a two-verb exit (vayaqam Shemuel vaya'al min hagilgal), with a pe sited after 13:14 in both witnesses. The front edge is weaker than previously stated: 13:8 opens with vayochel (ketiv/qere), a wayyiqtol with no expressed subject, retrievable only from 13:7's medial clause naming Saul (veshaul odenu bagilgal), with the verse's own final clause naming kol ha'am instead (vechol ha'am charedu acharav); in the immediately preceding stretch (13:5, 13:6, 13:7), this narrator marks every change of focus with waw plus a fronted subject, and the withholding of that construction exactly at this seam counts against a boundary here rather than for one. The unit's own claimed opening marker ('the shift from waiting to arrival') is span-internal - Saul waits at 13:8, Samuel arrives at 13:10 - and describes the scene's development, not its edge. Disclosure note: 13:15's departure clause sits at a juncture sometimes discussed as a point of versional divergence; the sources assigned to this campaign (MT-only OSHB, a WEB clean text with no footnote at 13:15, and a chapter-level verse-count crosswalk that is silent about intra-verse pluses) cannot confirm or deny this, so the specific claim of versional divergence is marked insufficient_evidence here.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting Saul's self-justification (vv.11-12) from Samuel's verdict (vv.13-14) was considered, but the two form one uninterrupted exchange in which Samuel's rebuke directly answers Saul's excuse without any scene gap. Extending the span backward to include 13:7b (so the unit begins with the disjunctive clause that supplies vayochel's subject) is a live alternative not adopted here, since 13:7 belongs to the preceding, out-of-half decision; downgrading confidence and naming the true (silent) front-edge juncture is preferred instead.

boundary_rationale: The watchmen at Gibeah see the melting multitude, Saul orders a headcount that reveals Jonathan's absence, and he initiates a consultation involving the ark or its attendant -- only to cut the ritual short mid-request as the tumult grows, closing on the interrupted 'Withdraw your hand!' before the muster proper begins. Disclosure note: the content of what Saul calls for is genuinely uncertain in MT. 14:18b's explanatory clause (ki hayah aron ha'Elohim bayom hahu uvenei Yisrael) joins 'the ark of God' and 'the sons of Israel' with a bare conjunction and no predicate, so WEB must supply a preposition ('was with') to yield sense; the immediate context also sits oddly with a physically-summoned ark, since 14:3 has already stationed the priest as nose efod ('bearer of an ephod') and Saul's 14:19 command, esof yadecha ('withdraw your hand'), addresses a gesture rather than a transported object. This crux is disclosed rather than resolved; it does not affect the span or its edges (a new vantage and new participants open at 14:16, a pe closes both 14:19 and this unit in both witnesses).

boundary_rationale: Saul's proposal to pursue by night meets the priest's counsel to inquire of God first, and God's silence triggers a lot-casting narrowing step by step from all Israel to Saul-and-Jonathan to Jonathan alone. The rear edge is weaker than previously rated: the seam at 14:42|14:43 is the sixth occurrence of the vayomer (Shaul) formula in eight verses (14:36, 14:38, 14:40 subjectless, 14:41, 14:42, 14:43), with nothing distinguishing the sixth from the fifth that the draft treats as internal; the span's final clause (vayilached Yonatan, 14:42) nearly repeats the outcome already given one verse earlier (vayilached Yonatan veShaul, 14:41), the profile of a resumption rather than a division. Disclosure note: the oracle request at 14:41, havah tamim ('give the perfect/complete one'), is two words naming one term, while the result clause immediately distinguishes two parties (Jonathan-and-Saul versus the people); WEB renders it 'Show the right' with no footnote, and the campaign's assigned sources cannot settle the fuller form of the request. The unit's internal narrowing sequence (all Israel to the royal pair to Jonathan) itself, rather than the procedure's 'formality,' is what argues for treating 14:36-14:42 as one unit; the front edge remains solid (the altar notice, a pe after 14:35, and a new proposal at 14:36).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the divine silence and diagnostic question (vv.37-38) from the lot-casting itself (vv.39-42) was considered, but they form one uninterrupted judicial procedure moving from failed inquiry to formal lot without any scene break. Closing instead at 14:40|14:41 or 14:45|14:46, where the witnesses actually place marks, is a live untested alternative not adopted here since the drafted span's own front edge and internal narrowing sequence remain the stronger overall account.

boundary_rationale: A war-catalog register opens with 'Now when Saul had taken the kingdom' and lists his enemies by name in a genuine five-member enumerated series, each introduced by the same preposition (bemoav uvivnei ammon uve'edom uvemalchei tzovah uvaplishtim, 14:47) -- a form distinct from both the oath-crisis narrative before it and the family register that follows. The list_register tag describes 14:47 cleanly but only half the span: 14:48 is three plain wayyiqtol clauses (vaya'as chayil vayach et Amalek vayatzel et Yisrael miyad shosehu) with no enumeration, formally indistinguishable from ordinary narrative summary; the two verses are held together by a samekh sited after 14:48 rather than by a shared register. The unit's actual closing clause is 14:48's vayatzel et Yisrael miyad shosehu ('he delivered Israel from the hand of him who plundered them'), not 14:47's uvechol asher yifneh yarshia -- a hiphil of r-sh-'a with no expressed object, whose base sense ('he condemned/acted wickedly') is rendered contextually by WEB as 'he defeated them,' an object supplied by the translation. A lexical hinge worth preserving: 14:47's vesha'ul lachad hamelucha ('Saul seized the kingship') reuses the root lachad just applied three times, passively, to Jonathan's capture by lot at 14:41-42 -- Saul seizes a kingship in the same verb by which his son was caught.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Combining the wars catalog with the family register into one closing-summary span was considered, but the two lists differ in kind -- military opponents versus kinship names -- and the text itself marks a fresh start at v.49 with 'Now the sons of Saul were.' Splitting 14:47 (catalogue) from 14:48 (narrative coda) into two decisions was also considered and declined, since a samekh after 14:48 corroborates keeping them together even though only one verse carries the list-register form.

boundary_rationale: A family register names Saul's sons and daughters, his wife Ahinoam, his army commander, and a note on the commander's father, a closed genealogical form opening on 'Now the sons of Saul were' and closing before the chapter's final generalizing refrain. The genuine shared-grandfather relationship (Kish is elsewhere named ben Aviel at 9:1) is a cross-chapter inference, not the content of 14:51 taken alone, and is now stated as such. A smaller orthographic note preserved from the source check: MT spells the commander's name Avinner at 14:50 and Avner at 14:51, two forms one verse apart.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this list through the closing war-refrain (v.52) was considered, but v.52 shifts from naming individuals to a durative, unnamed-scope statement about lifelong warfare, a register change from genealogy to summary.

Both edges remain well-marked: a samekh sited after both 14:51 and 14:52, the register plainly changing from named individuals to an unbounded statement, and 15:1 beginning a fresh commissioning speech.

boundary_rationale: Yahweh's word comes to Samuel using the root that will bracket the whole chapter - 'It grieves me [nichamti] that I have set up Saul' (15:11) - opening the chapter's inclusio (matched by 15:35's vaYHWH nicham), and the unit closes with Samuel's all-night cry and the morning report of his setting out to meet Saul. Genre-wise this span is majority narration framing a single clause of oracle: 15:10 is a bare word-event formula (vayehi devar YHWH el Shemuel lemor) with no speech content of its own; only 15:11a (nichamti...lo hekim) is first-person divine speech; and 15:11b-15:12 return to pure third-person narration - v.12 alone contains five wayyiqtols (vayashkem, vayuggad, vayissov, vaya'avor, vayered) reporting Samuel's grief, his cry, and his search for Saul. Tagged accordingly as narrative_and_prophetic_oracle rather than prophetic_oracle_speech, paralleling M8-1Sam-177's compound tag for a span with the opposite proportion (majority oracle there; majority narration here). The near edge is the strongest in this cluster: 15:10 opens the dedicated word-event formula vayehi devar YHWH el Shemuel lemor, corroborated by a pe after 15:9. The far edge is weaker than previously rated: 15:12 states Samuel's purpose (liqrat Shaul, 'to meet Saul') and 15:13 executes it (vayavo Shemuel el Shaul) with the same subject and no intervening narration, joined by a bare wayyiqtol - a journey-to-arrival split, the weakest kind of seam. Citation correction: 15:11's nacham anchor is content evidence for the chapter's inclusio, not edge evidence for this span's own boundary, and is cited here accordingly rather than among the boundary markers.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding Samuel's night-long cry into the confrontation scene that follows was considered, but the cry and the search for Saul the next morning belong to Samuel's private response before any dialogue with Saul begins. A stronger high-confidence unit in this neighborhood, if wanted, belongs to the decision covering 15:13 onward (outside this half's manifest), whose two edges are both independently marked; that observation does not change this decision's own span.

boundary_rationale: Saul's confession and plea for pardon are met by Samuel's refusal and departure, the torn-robe sign-act, and the declaration 'Yahweh has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today.' The near edge is genuinely strong, corroborated by the samekh after 15:23 at the exit from the poetic couplet. The far edge is weaker than previously rated: 15:24 opens with vayomer Shaul el Shemuel chatati ('Saul said to Samuel, I have sinned') and 15:30, immediately past this span, opens vayomer chatati - the identical verb and confession word, with the speaker recoverable only from inside the closing span - a resumption signal rather than a division; the nearest samekh, after 15:26, sits span-internal. The closing counter-statement, 'the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent' (15:29, lo yeshaqer velo yinachem), is correctly read as ironic, but the irony runs through the nacham root's own three appearances - Yahweh's first-person grief at 15:11 (nichamti), its emphatic denial here at 15:29, and the narrator's reassertion at 15:35 (vaYHWH nicham) - not through Samuel's night-long response at 15:11, which is built on the unrelated roots ch-r-h ('was angry') and z-'-q ('cried out').
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the torn-robe sign-act (v.27) from its accompanying declaration (v.28) was considered, but the physical tearing and the verbal 'Yahweh has torn' pronouncement are presented as one symbolic gesture-plus-word event. Closing this unit earlier, at 15:26 (where a samekh does sit) rather than at 15:29, is a live alternative not adopted, since the torn-robe sign-act and its declaration (vv.27-29) form one continuous symbolic sequence with the refusal that precedes it.

boundary_rationale: Goliath's introduction gives way to an itemized armor description running vv.5-7 as an unbroken chain of waw-plus-noun clauses -- wekhova' nechosheth, weshiryon qasqassim, umitschath nechosheth, wekhidon nechosheth, we'ets chanito (qere; ketiv vechets), welahevet chanito, wenose' hatsinnah -- with consecutive narration resuming only at v.8 (wayya'amod). Only two of the five itemized pieces (the coat at 5,000 shekels, the spear's head at 600 shekels) carry an actual weight; the helmet, greaves, and kidon carry none, and the 'weaver's beam' line is a simile, not a measure -- the earlier claim that each piece 'is given its own weight or measure' overstated the text and is withdrawn. boundary_rationale: The combat itself -- the run, the sling, the fatal strike, the beheading with Goliath's own sword -- forms the story's physical climax, opening on 'the Philistine arose' (wehayah ki qam happelishti) and closing on the Philistines' flight once they see their champion is dead. The unit contains its own internal doublet, disclosed here rather than smoothed over: v.50 narrates the kill with the sling and stone and explicitly notes 'there was no sword in David's hand' (wayemitehu, wecherev 'en beyad dawid), while v.51 has David draw Goliath's own sword and kill him a second time with it (wayemotetehu, using a different causative form of the same root). This is the same kind of doublet pattern the campaign discloses at 18:10-12 versus 19:9-10, here internal to a single span; it does not move the unit's edges, since both verses belong to the same uninterrupted combat scene, but the tension is real and should not be described as an unqualified 'unmistakable turning point' without naming it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this through the pursuit and plunder (vv.52-54) was considered, but the flight notice at the end of v.51 is the direct trigger for the pursuit that follows, and the shift from single combat to a mass battle scene marks a real change of scale. Treating vv.50 and 51 as two separate decisions was not considered necessary, since both are part of one continuous combat scene; the internal weapon-detail doublet is disclosed above rather than used to argue for a respan.

boundary_rationale: Saul's question to Abner about David's identity closes the chapter on a note that sits awkwardly beside chapter 16's introduction of David to Saul's own household staff. Two live readings of that tension should both be named rather than only one: a source-critical reading (this material's relationship to other textual traditions, which this packet's supplied sources -- WEB, OSHB, the verse crosswalk, and the two-witness apparatus -- cannot adjudicate, since no Greek witness is present anywhere in this packet) and a purely literary reading, in which Saul's failure to recognize a servant he supposedly already loves is coherent characterization given his affliction already established at 16:14 ('Yahweh's Spirit departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from Yahweh troubled him'), rather than only a seam from an unharmonized source layer. The unit itself opens on a vantage-shift disjunctive, wekhir'oth sha'ul (v.55), and closes on the chapter-final question-and-answer exchange (v.58) naming David's father.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating vv.55-58 as continuous with the pursuit-and-plunder unit before it was considered, but the shift in vantage from the battlefield to Saul watching David from a distance, and the reopening of a question chapter 16 seemed to have already settled, marks a distinct closing unit. The earlier ground for that reopened-question tension (an asserted Septuagint minus) is withdrawn as unsourced; the psychological reading (Saul's affliction from 16:14 already accounts for an unstable memory) is now named alongside it as an unresolved, live alternative rather than treated as settled by the text-critical claim.

boundary_rationale: The unit opens on wayehi bevo'am beshuv dawid mehakkoth 'eth happelishti (v.6), a temporal-anchor construction introducing a new participant group -- the women of the cities -- and runs through their antiphonal couplet in v.7 ('Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands') to Saul's angry monologue (v.8) and the durative notice that Saul watched David from that day forward (v.9, wayehi sha'ul 'oyen 'eth dawid). The couplet itself, embedded within this narrative unit, is set off in the WEB source by its own q1/q2 line markers, but that formatting cannot itself drive the unit's type or boundary: the actual poetic signal is the Hebrew bicolon's own parallel constituents and numerical escalation (hikkah sha'ul ba'alafaw, wedawid berivvothaw). boundary_rationale: The first of two javelin episodes -- an evil spirit comes on Saul, he prophesies in his house while David plays, and Saul hurls his spear (a single cast, wayyatel sha'ul 'eth hachanith) while David escapes his presence twice (wayyissov dawid mippanaw pa'amayim) -- is a compact, self-contained scene closing on the narrator's explanation that Saul feared David because Yahweh had left him. This episode's near-verbatim counterpart recurs at 19:9-10 (cited below), and this campaign's doublet discipline treats each as its own genuine event rather than collapsing them; the javelin motif in fact recurs a third time, still more closely in wording, at 20:33 (wayyatel sha'ul 'eth hachanith 'alaw lehakotho -- the identical opening four words), making this a three-member motif set (18:10-12; 19:8-10; 20:30-34) rather than a simple pair.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging this with Saul's subsequent demotion of David (vv.13-16) was considered, but the demotion is a distinct administrative response narrated with its own new opening ('Therefore Saul removed him'), not a continuation of the spear-throwing scene itself. Collapsing this scene with 19:9-10 into a single cross-chapter span was also considered and rejected, since the two are narrated as separate dated incidents with different immediate consequences (demotion here, permanent flight there); the near-verbatim characterization is corrected to note that this scene shares only a partial formula with 19:9-10 (the evil-spirit-comes clause and the melee-with-David clause) but shares its opening four words verbatim with the later, third instance at 20:33.

boundary_rationale: War resumes and David's renewed success is followed immediately by the second javelin episode, opening on the evil spirit's return (wattehi ruach YHWH ra'ah 'el sha'ul) and closing on David's flight into the night, the episode that precipitates his permanent break with the court. This shares a three-element core with 18:10-12 (the evil-spirit-comes-on-Saul clause; 'David playing music with his hand'; the bedawid uvaqqir strike-formula) but is not a near-verbatim copy: the divine name and verb differ (wattitslach...'elohim at 18:10 vs. wattehi...YHWH here), 18:10's 'he prophesied in the house' clause is absent here, and the casting verb differs (wayyatel...'akkeh at 18:11 vs. wayevaqqesh lehakkoth here). This campaign's doublet discipline treats each as its own genuine, dated event rather than collapsing them; the motif in fact forms a three-member set with 20:30-34 (wayyatel sha'ul 'eth hachanith 'alaw lehakotho, verbally the closest match to 18:11's opening four words), not merely this two-member pair.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Collapsing this with 18:10-12 into a single cross-chapter span on the grounds of their near-verbatim parallel was considered and rejected, since the two are narrated as separate dated incidents with different immediate consequences -- the first ends in demotion, this one in flight. The relation is now described as a shared three-element formula inside materially different frames, and the fuller motif set (including 20:33's closer verbal match) is disclosed rather than treated as a simple pair.

boundary_rationale: Saul's messengers surround David's house, and Michal's teraphim ruse buys time for his escape through the window; the unit closes on her confrontation with her father, a bounded rescue-and-deception scene opening on the night watch and closing on Michal's self-protective lie to Saul. The escape itself is completed by the end of v.12 (a three-verb sequence: wayyelekh wayyivrach wayyimmalet, 'he went, fled, and escaped'), and only then does Michal stage the teraphim in the bed (v.13) as a delaying cover for an escape already made, not as preparation enabling it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the physical escape (vv.11-12) from the teraphim deception and its discovery (vv.13-17) was considered; the earlier ground for rejecting that split (that the ruse was prepared before the escape was complete) is corrected, since the text has the opposite order. The split is nonetheless still rejected, on the accurate ground that the whole sequence -- the messengers' night watch, David's completed escape, and Michal's delaying cover story -- functions as one coordinated rescue with a single deceptive object (the teraphim) at its center, resolving in her confrontation with Saul.

boundary_rationale: Saul himself goes to Naioth, is overcome by the same prophetic Spirit, strips his clothes, and lies prophesying all day and night, closing on a distant etiological reprise of the proverb first coined at 10:11-12, 'Is Saul also among the prophets?' This is a distant reprise rather than an inclusio (the two occurrences bracket nine intervening chapters, not this unit), so the genuinely independent support for this unit's own closing edge is the chapter-final position itself together with a two-witness pe after 19:24 -- not the recurrence's borrowed force. The closer formal partner for the proverb-formation is 10:12 ('al ken hayethah lemashal, 'therefore it became a proverb'), which matches this verse's own 'al ken yo'meru ('therefore they say') more precisely than 10:11 does; the wording is identical at the qere/translation level but is spelled three different ways across the three consonantal printings (10:11 plene; 10:12 and 19:24 each with their own distinct defective spelling).

boundary_rationale: The next morning the arrow signal is enacted, the boy is dismissed, and David and Jonathan meet for a final embrace and renewed oath 'between me and you, and between my offspring and your offspring, forever' (v.42, ending 'ad 'olam), closing the whole covenant sequence. Two disclosures follow from fresh verification of the underlying texts. First, this span's closing edge crosses the Masoretic chapter division without a dual citation: MT 1Sam.20.42 ends at 'ad 'olam, and the clause WEB prints as the remainder of the same verse -- 'He arose and departed; and Jonathan went into the city' -- is a separate verse in the Hebrew, MT 1Sam.21.1. This is the literal mechanical origin of chapter 21's mt_extra_1 status (WEB 15 verses vs. MT 16) recorded in web_mt_crosswalk.json; the crosswalk's chapter-20 'identical' relation (42/42) is a count-level artifact that conceals this content-level seam at the chapter's last verse. The closing edge is accordingly dual-cited below as WEB 1Sam.20.42 = MT 1Sam.20.42 + MT 1Sam.21.1, and the span is kept as drawn (WEB's own numbering is this campaign's citation register), rather than redrawn. A two-witness pe follows MT 20:42 -- i.e., it falls between the oath content and the departure clause, inside WEB's merged verse, and corroborates the MT chapter break rather than this span's WEB-numbered edge; disclosed rather than treated as supporting the drafted boundary at face value. Second, the claim that the arrow signal was enacted 'exactly as planned' is corrected: the plan specifies three arrows and a plural danger call (v.20, v.22), while the actual shooting is narrated with a singular arrow throughout (v.36, v.37), a plan/enactment divergence in number that v.38's own ketiv/qere (singular written, plural read) preserves rather than resolves.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the mechanical signal (vv.35-38) from the emotional farewell (vv.39-42) was considered, but the boy's ignorance of the code's real meaning is explicitly contrasted with what David and Jonathan alone know, binding the signal and the private farewell into one scene the boy's departure clears the stage for. The span is retained across the MT 20:42/21:1 seam rather than truncated at 'ad 'olam, since WEB's own verse numbering is the citation register this campaign uses throughout; what changes is disclosure, not the boundary.

boundary_rationale: This single verse is an explanatory aside noting that Abiathar arrived at Keilah with an ephod in hand, supplying the mechanism the narrative will need for the oracular inquiries that follow in vv.9-12. Its isolating signal is not, as previously argued, a resemblance to the reader-directed terminology gloss at 9:9 (a different construction: lefanim plus an explanatory frame) -- the verse's own opening, wayehi bivroach, is an ordinary wayehi-plus-infinitive construction that elsewhere in this book opens perfectly ordinary main-line episodes (e.g. 25:2, 30:1) and carries no backgrounding force by itself. boundary_rationale: David's move to the wilderness of Ziph opens a new phase of pursuit, and Jonathan's secret visit there provides a third covenant renewal - 'you will be king over Israel, and I will be next to you' - closing on their mutual covenant before Yahweh and Jonathan's return home. This unit is not textured uniformly throughout: vv.14-15a form a general summary of David's fugitive condition, closing on a verbless disjunctive ('וְדָוִ֥ד בְּמִדְבַּר זִ֖יף בַּחֹֽרְשָׁה,' 'David was in the wilderness of Ziph in the woods'), while vv.15b-18 stage the specific, located Jonathan-visit episode. Chorshah ('the woods') recurs at all three of v.15 (bachorshah, closing the summary), v.16 (chorshah, opening the located episode), and v.18 (bachorshah, closing the covenant); its recurrence is weak corroboration of the whole unit's continuity across all three verses, not proof that binds only the second beat. A WEB paragraph break (immediately before v.16) and a two-witness samekh (after MT 23:15) corroborate treating vv.14-15a and vv.15b-18 as two beats within this larger unit, rather than reading the whole span as textured uniformly. boundary_rationale: Samuel's death and burial notice is a self-contained obituary formula recurring in content (though not in grammatical construction) with the later reminder at 28:3, standing apart from both the En Gedi narrative just concluded and the Nabal story David's relocation to Paran opens. This verse is a wayyiqtol chain of six coordinated verbs (wayyamoth Shemu'el, wayyiqqavtsu, wayyispedu, wayyiqberuhu bevaitho baramah, 'Samuel died...and buried him at his house at Ramah,' then wayyaqom David, wayyered el midbar Paran, 'David arose and went down to the wilderness of Paran,' the relocation clause folding David's departure into the same notice), not a regnal-type notice: it carries no accession formula, reign-length figure, or succession clause, and its construction is the opposite of 28:3's own double waw-plus-subject-plus-qatal disjunctive. Retyped as narrative_prose accordingly; the relation to 28:3 is one of shared content (death, mourning, burial) rather than shared grammatical form. Disclosure, as weak corroborating metadata rather than a driver of this decision: WEB places its own paragraph break mid-verse, between the burial notice and 'Then David arose,' and a two-witness samekh sits at this verse's own rear edge (1Sam.25.1); neither is load-bearing for the boundary, which rests on the verse's self-contained obituary-plus-relocation content.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching the relocation clause to the following Nabal exposition (vv.2-3) was considered, but the obituary and the relocation are reported as one compact notice functioning as a hinge -- confirmed by v.2's own verbless disjunctive opening ('we'ish bema'on,' 'there was a man in Maon'), which begins the Nabal exposition proper only after this verse closes -- not as the start of the Nabal narrative's own character introductions.

strongest_rejected_alternative: Separating the provisioning list (v.18) from David's oath (vv.21-22) was considered, but both are bound together by Abigail's journey toward the encounter that the oath anticipates, forming one build-up unit before they actually meet.

strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating vv.23-31 as one undivided speech was considered, but the shift at v.28 from apology and gift-presentation to forward-looking theological argument about David's 'sure house' and future kingship marks a distinct rhetorical movement worth its own unit.

boundary_rationale: Abigail's speech turns from apology to theological and political argument -- Yahweh will make David 'a sure house,' his life is 'bound in the bundle of life,' and he is destined to be 'prince over Israel' -- closing on her forward-looking plea that he remember her once Yahweh has dealt well with him. The turn itself does not fall cleanly at the 27/28 boundary: v.28 is a compound verse, opening with the apology petition itself ('please forgive the trespass of your servant') before turning, in its second half, to the sure-house promise. Since spans are drawn at verse granularity, v.28 is assigned to this forward-looking unit because its dominant and longer content is the dynastic argument that continues through v.31, not because a clean formal break falls at 27/28.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping this as the closing section of one long undivided speech-span was considered, but the argument's content does shift, over the course of v.28, from present request to future destiny -- a change in rhetorical aim the campaign's binding rules treat as a legitimate internal seam, even though that shift completes inside v.28 rather than exactly at its boundary.

boundary_rationale: Nabal's drunken feast, Abigail's delayed disclosure the next morning, and the onset of what reads as a stroke followed by his death ten days later at Yahweh's hand form a tightly sequenced three-beat unit closing the Nabal half of the story. Two wayehi-plus-temporal markers sit inside this three-verse span -- wayehi babboqer at v.37 and, separately, wayehi ka'asereth hayyamim at v.38, a larger displacement (ten days against one morning). Both are disposed of rather than only one: the emphatic double-scope negation at v.36 ('she told him not a word, small or great, until the morning light') is answered directly by the morning collapse in the very next verse, and the ten-day marker at v.38 is the narrated delayed outcome of that same stroke -- Yahweh's striking of Nabal and his death are one causal event reported across two verses (the onset in v.37, the fatal end ten days later in v.38), not an independent new scene requiring its own boundary.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the feast and delayed telling (v.36) from the death itself (vv.37-38) was considered, but the delay is explicitly narrated as a deliberate choice whose payoff is the collapse in the very next verse. A further split isolating v.38's own ten-day marker was also considered, since that wayehi-plus-temporal frame is treated as seam evidence elsewhere in this range (30:1, 27:7, 31:8); it is subordinated here because the stroke (v.37) and the death (v.38) are one continuous causal sequence -- onset and fatal outcome of the same divinely-caused event -- not two separately triggered scenes.

boundary_rationale: The chapter closes with two matched marital/annalistic notices, each built on a suspended clause -- v.43 fronts its object (we'eth 'achino'am laqach dawid, 'David also took Ahinoam') and v.44 fronts its subject (wesha'ul nathan, 'Saul had given...') -- a matched syntactic pair rather than a lineage chain or begetting formula, so 'genealogical_register' is retyped as an annalistic-notice class. V.43's own wording ('gam shteihen,' 'also, the two of them') explicitly reaches back to the Abigail marriage just narrated; this is acknowledged as a genuine semantic tie across the 42/43 seam, but it is retained as texture rather than treated as grounds to relocate v.43 into the preceding unit, since the matched fronted-clause syntax of vv.43-44 is what actually binds this pair together as its own closing unit -- and a two-witness samekh falls between the two verses, an alternative (a 43/44 split) the earlier rejected alternative never named.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging these notices into the Abigail marriage unit was considered -- v.43's own 'also, the two of them' explicitly backreferences that marriage -- but the matched fronted-clause syntax linking v.43 and v.44 argues for keeping them as their own paired unit rather than folding v.43 backward. A split between v.43 and v.44 was also considered, since a two-witness samekh falls precisely between them, but is subordinated to the syntactic pairing, which binds the two verses together as parallel suspended-clause notices closing the chapter.

The report shares a six-word core with 23:19 ('to Saul at Gibeah, saying, Does not David hide himself') plus the Hachilah toponym, but is a compressed restatement rather than a near-copy: the main verb changes (wayya'alu -> wayyavo'u), the subject gains the article, the entire 'with us, in the strongholds, in Horesh' locative sequence present at 23:19 is dropped, and the hayeshimon modifier is recast.

The two reports are narrated as distinct, re-triggered episodes, so this occurrence opens its own unit rather than extending the earlier one; the near-verbatim characterization of their relationship is corrected as above.

boundary_rationale: The night infiltration of Saul's camp is a self-contained scene -- Abishai's volunteering, David's restraint speech invoking Yahweh's anointed, and the taking of the spear and water jar as silent proof -- opening on David's question 'Who will go down with me' and closing on the notice that a deep sleep from Yahweh had fallen on the whole camp. The exchange is not, in fact, wholly uninterrupted: David's speech is introduced twice with wayyomer dawid (v.9, addressing Abishai directly; v.10, resuming without any intervening answer from Abishai), and a two-witness pe falls exactly at that join. This doubled introduction is read as rhetorical emphasis -- David silencing Abishai's proposal and restating his own reasoning at greater length -- rather than a compositional seam, since the whole exchange still resolves directly into the action David proposes without any change of scene, location, or participants.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting Abishai's offer to kill Saul (vv.8-9) from the taking of the relics (vv.11-12) was considered; the earlier ground for rejecting that split (an uninterrupted exchange) is corrected, since v.9 and v.10 each reintroduce David with wayyomer dawid and no answering turn from Abishai stands between them, with a two-witness pe marking that seam. The split is nonetheless still rejected: the doubled introduction reads as David's own emphatic restatement rather than a change of scene, and the whole passage resolves directly into the action it proposes.

boundary_rationale: This verse is its own setting notice, built from two waw-plus-subject-plus-qatal clauses in succession (ushemu'el meth, 'Now Samuel was dead'; wesha'ul hesir, 'and Saul had put away the mediums and wizards') -- a double disjunctive standing alone between Achish's direct speech ending at v.2 and the wayyiqtol narrative restart at v.4 ('the Philistines gathered'), which is what actually isolates this verse as a narrator-time island, background necessary for the Endor scene about to unfold. The verse recurs in content (Samuel's death, Israel's mourning, burial) with 25:1, but the two notices are not structurally parallel: 25:1 is a wayyiqtol chain of four coordinated verbs, the opposite construction, and the two do not even agree on the burial location ('at his house at Ramah' at 25:1; 'in Ramah, even in his own city' here). The relation to 25:1 is one of content recurrence only, not shared grammatical form. Per the campaign's own known observation about this Endor material, this verse also sits at the seam where the muster-formula bracket opened at 28:1 ('the Philistines gathered their armies') and closed at 29:1 (the near-identical resumption after the Endor cutaway) begins its interruption.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this reminder into the muster notice that follows (vv.4-7) was considered, but the verse's entirely retrospective content -- what has already happened, not what is now happening -- together with its double waw-plus-subject-plus-qatal disjunctive construction standing alone between the end of direct speech (v.2) and the wayyiqtol restart (v.4), marks it as a distinct scene-setting unit rather than the start of the new military narrative. The earlier ground for isolating it (a claimed structural parallel to 25:1) is withdrawn as unsupported; the syntactic argument above is sufficient on its own.

strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this to the actual approach to the woman at Endor (vv.8-14) was considered, but v.8 opens a new scene with a change of location and Saul's own disguise, a deliberate concealment absent from the muster-and-inquiry unit before it.

boundary_rationale: Saul's disguised night approach to the medium at Endor opens a necromantic type-scene structured by negotiation, then summons, then a doubly-mediated apparition sequence: the woman alone perceives what rises and reports it to Saul in stages (first 'a god coming up out of the earth,' then 'an old man...covered with a robe'), and Saul's own recognition of Samuel at v.14 is an inference from her secondhand description rather than direct perception. The scene in fact contains two recognition beats in inverted order -- the medium recognizes Saul first, crying out 'Why have you deceived me? For you are Saul!' the moment she perceives whatever appears (v.12), and only afterward does Saul, working from her description, infer that the apparition is Samuel (v.14) -- closing when he bows to the ground. This mediated-access structure, with recognition running in reversed order, sharpens rather than undermines the case for treating vv.8-14 as an unusual and unmistakably bounded episode within the history's otherwise ordinary prose.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the negotiation over safety (vv.9-10) from the summoning and apparition itself (vv.11-14) was considered, but the woman's swearing of safety is presented as the direct precondition that unlocks the summons she performs immediately afterward.

boundary_rationale: Samuel's appearance opens with a two-turn dialogue at v.15 (Samuel's question, 'Why have you disturbed me, to bring me up?', met by Saul's four-clause complaint that closes with his reason for consulting the medium at all), rather than oracle proper. The oracle itself begins at v.16 with a fresh speech frame, vayomer Shemuel, and delivers the doom pronouncement that explicitly reprises the 'Yahweh has torn the kingdom' language first spoken at 15:28 (compare qara YHWH et mamlekhuth Yisra'el me'aleikha...lere'akha hattov mimmekka at 15:28 with vayyiqra YHWH et hammamlakhah miyadekha vayyitnah lere'akha leDavid at 28:17 - the same three roots, qr'/mmlkh/ntn, in the same order, now naming the beneficiary outright), closing on the specific, dated prediction that Saul and his sons will be with Samuel 'tomorrow.' The join's evidence, recounted honestly: the drivers are the fresh vayomer-Shemuel speech frame reopening at 28:16 and the oracle's own content (the 15:28/28:17 reprise); a two-witness samekh after MT 28:15 corroborates the seam, but only weakly, per this book's own rule for corroborating marks; and WEB's own paragraphing, which independently breaks both mid-verse-15 and again before v.16, is disclosed here as metadata only (modern paragraphing, not an independent text signal) rather than counted among the converging signals.

boundary_rationale: The Philistine muster at Aphek opens with David and his men marching in the rear alongside Achish, and the princes' objecting speech -- reprising the same victory-song refrain already quoted at 18:7 and again at 21:11 (=oshb 21:12; the earlier bare '21:11' reference is corrected here, since MT 21:11 is in fact the flight-to-Gath verse, not the refrain) -- closes the unit on their demand that David be sent back before the army moves further. This is the refrain's third occurrence, a genuine triple rather than a pair, identical at the reading (qere) level across all three sites but printed with different ketiv/qere marking at each (18:7 marks only the first colon; 21:11/oshb 21:12 marks both cola; 29:5 marks only the second). This verse also completes the resumptive-repetition bracket opened at 28:1 ('the Philistines gathered their armies,' wayyiqbetsu pelishtim 'eth machaneihem) and closed here at 29:1 ('the Philistines gathered all their armies to Aphek,' wayyiqbetsu pelishtim 'eth kol machaneihem 'afeqah) -- a four-word shared core marking the whole Endor sequence (28:3-25) as a deliberate bracketed insertion within the Achish thread rather than a loosely sequenced addition.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the princes' initial complaint (vv.3-4) from their citation of the song (v.5) was considered, but the song is quoted as the clinching piece of evidence within their single continuous objection, not as a separate speech act.

boundary_rationale: The pursuit to the brook Besor, the two hundred men left behind, and the discovery of an abandoned Egyptian slave form a rescued-informant type-scene, opening on the march itself and closing on the Egyptian's sworn promise to guide David to the raiding party in exchange for his life.

boundary_rationale: The Egyptian leads David to the raiders, found feasting and dancing over their plunder, and the resulting battle runs through a closural fronted-object summary pair at vv.18-19 ('David rescued his two wives'; 'David brought them all back,' hakkol heshiv dawid) before the unit's actual final beat: David's own act of claiming the recovered livestock as personal plunder at v.20, a wayyiqtol restart ('David took all the flocks and the herds...and said, This is David's plunder,' zeh shelal dawid). This is the unit's true closing content -- the earlier description, which quoted 'David brought them all back' as the close, was in fact quoting v.19, one verse short of the cited edge. V.20's naming of the flocks and herds as 'David's plunder' introduces the very term (shelal) the following unit's distribution dispute depends on ('the plunder that we have recovered,' v.22).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the discovery and battle (vv.16-17) from the recovery notice (vv.18-20) was considered, but the recovery is presented as the direct and immediate result of the battle just fought, without any narrated interruption between combat and its outcome. A split between the recovery summary (vv.16-19, closing on 'David brought them all back') and David's own plunder-claiming act (v.20) was also considered, since vv.18-19 read as a closural cadence in their own right; it is subordinated here because v.20's naming of the livestock as 'David's plunder' is the direct antecedent the wicked men's complaint in the next unit depends on, and keeping it within this unit preserves that connection rather than splitting a two-verse transition awkwardly.

boundary_rationale: David reunites with the two hundred left at Besor, and the wicked men's proposal to deny them any share of the plunder is overruled by David's own ruling establishing equal shares for those who fight and those who guard the baggage, closing on the explicit statute-and-ordinance formula 'to this day' (v.25, wayesimeha lechoq ulemishpat leyisra'el 'ad hayyom hazzeh) that gives this unit a legal, precedent-setting character distinct from the battle narrative before it. V.25 opens on its own wayehi-plus-temporal frame and moves into the narrator's own present, and is fenced on both sides by two-witness marks (a samekh after v.24, a pe after v.25) -- stronger apparatus corroboration than most seams in this range carry. This alternative (isolating the statute notice itself) is named and subordinated explicitly: David's ruling (v.24) and the statute it becomes (v.25) are treated here as one continuous legal act -- the ruling is the substance, and v.25 is its codification and durative naming -- rather than as two independent topics warranting separate spans.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding the plunder-distribution list to Judah's elders (vv.26-31) into this unit was considered, but that list concerns an entirely separate act of generosity to towns outside the army, introduced by its own 'When David came to Ziklag' clause. A split isolating the statute notice itself (v.25) was also considered, since it opens on a wayehi-plus-temporal frame, moves into narrator-time language ('to this day'), and is fenced by two-witness marks on both sides (samekh after v.24, pe after v.25); it is subordinated here because David's ruling and the statute it becomes are one continuous legal act rather than two independent topics.

boundary_rationale: The battle on Mount Gilboa opens the book's final chapter, moving through the deaths of Saul's sons, his own mortal wounding, his request that his armor-bearer kill him, the bearer's refusal, and Saul's own suicide followed by the bearer's - closing on the summary that Saul died 'with his three sons... and all his men that same day together,' a bounded death scene with an unmistakable closing cadence.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting Saul's death (vv.4-5) from the summary notice (v.6) was considered, but the summary functions as the direct concluding tally of the same event just narrated, not a separate report.

boundary_rationale: News of the defeat triggers a wider Israelite abandonment of cities across the valley and beyond the Jordan, and the unit shifts to the Philistines' discovery and desecration of Saul's body -- stripped armor displayed in the house of Ashtaroth, his corpse fastened to the wall of Beth Shan -- closing on that public humiliation before Jabesh Gilead's rescue mission begins. V.7 itself carries no temporal marker of any kind (a plain wayyiqtol chain: 'they saw...they abandoned...they fled'); it is v.8 that opens with its own wayehi-plus-temporal frame, 'on the next day' (wayehi mimmochorath), introducing the Philistines' arrival to strip the slain. A two-witness samekh falls after MT 31:7, agreeing that a seam of some kind runs at that point, but the Israelite flight (v.7) is kept with the desecration material here as one continuous account of the battle's aftermath -- a distinct, wider-scope consequence of the defeat regardless of when the Philistines arrive to strip the bodies -- rather than folded back into the battle narrative of vv.1-6.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching the flight of the Israelites (v.7) to the battle scene before it was considered; the earlier ground for rejecting that (that v.7 is reported 'only on the next day') is corrected, since that temporal marker belongs to v.8, not v.7, which has none. The flight (v.7) is nonetheless still kept with vv.8-10 rather than with vv.1-6, since it is a separate, wider-scope consequence of the defeat -- reported once the battle and Saul's death are already complete -- and the desecration material that follows continues that same aftermath.

boundary_rationale: Jabesh Gilead's valiant men - repaying the loyalty Saul first showed them in chapter 11 - make a night rescue of the bodies from Beth Shan's wall and give them proper burial with a seven-day mourning fast, closing the book without any colophon or forward-looking notice; the narrative of Israel's kingship simply continues into the opening verses of 2 Samuel, and this campaign treats the book's edge as an open narrative continuation rather than a closed unit requiring its own summary formula.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating this closing act as requiring some kind of terminal 'book summary' span of its own was considered, but 1 Samuel supplies no such formula - unlike, for instance, the regnal notices scattered through the book - and the honest reading is that the burial and mourning simply end the narrative in medias res, with the throne's fate left for the next scroll.
